title: Disaggregated prefill and decode
summary: Why prefill and decode interfere on shared GPUs, how goodput under TTFT and TPOT SLOs is measured, what moving the KV cache costs, and when splitting phases beats chunked prefill.
outcomes: Explain why mixing compute-bound prefill with memory-bound decode inflates TTFT and TPOT on a shared GPU
Compute SLO attainment and per-GPU goodput from latency measurements and a rate sweep
Compute KV transfer time from model config, prompt length and link bandwidth, and check sustained bandwidth
Explain how DistServe, Splitwise and Mooncake size, place and connect prefill and decode pools
Choose between chunked prefill and disaggregation for a given workload, SLO and interconnect

lessons.title: Why prefill stalls decode on a shared GPU

blocks.md:
Recall from the KV cache course: a request runs in two phases. **Prefill** pushes the whole prompt through the model in one forward pass, writes every prompt token's keys and values into the KV cache, and produces the first output token. **Decode** then generates one token per step, reading the whole KV cache each time.

The two phases use the GPU very differently. A prefill of a few hundred tokens or more is *compute-bound*: DistServe reports that a single 512-token prompt nearly saturates an A100 for a 13B model. A decode step does almost the same weight reads as a prefill but only one token of math per request, so it is *memory-bandwidth-bound*.

Two latency numbers follow from the two phases. DistServe (Zhong et al., OSDI 2024) defines:

- **TTFT** (time to first token): the time from arrival until prefill finishes and the first token appears.
- **TPOT** (time per output token): the average time per generated token after the first one.

Splitwise calls the per-step gap **TBT** (time between tokens), Mooncake uses TBT too, and vLLM's docs say **ITL** (inter-token latency). TPOT is an average over a request; TBT and ITL are usually looked at per step, which makes a single long stall visible.

blocks.caption: Each phase controls one term. DistServe's footnote writes it with TPOT times the tokens generated in the decoding phase.

blocks.md: Modern engines use **continuous batching**: every iteration, the scheduler mixes the prefill of newly arrived prompts with one decode step of every running request. That keeps the GPU busy, but now both phases share one iteration time. The figure uses a simplified cost model taken from Sarathi-Serve's roofline view, $T=\max(T_{math}, T_{mem})$: an iteration costs $\max(15 + 0.2B,\ 0.1(P+B))$ ms for $P$ prefill tokens and $B$ decoding requests. The constants are made up for illustration, not measured.

blocks.title: One prompt arrives while 16 requests are decoding

scenes.caption: 16 requests are decoding. Each step costs max(15 + 0.2 x 16, 0.1 x 16) = 18.2 ms, so every running request gets a token every 18.2 ms. A new 1024-token prompt C arrives at t = 30 ms.
The next iteration carries C's whole prefill plus the 16 decode steps: max(18.2, 0.1 x 1040) = 104 ms. Every running request waits 104 ms for its next token instead of 18.2 ms.
C's first token appears at 140.4 ms, so its TTFT is 110.4 ms (6.4 ms queueing plus 104 ms of work). Decoding resumes with 17 requests at 18.4 ms per step. One prompt cost 16 users a 5.7x longer gap.

blocks.md:
This is **prefill-decode interference**, and it goes both ways. DistServe measured that adding one prefill to a decode batch slows the decodes (longer TPOT), and the slowdown grows with prompt length. Adding decode work to a prefill also stretches it (longer TTFT) once the GPU is saturated.

Scheduling the phases in separate iterations does not fix it either: decodes then queue behind prefills, and prioritizing one phase hurts the other.

blocks.prompt: DistServe served a 13B model (prompts of 512 tokens, 64 output tokens) on one A100 and found about 1.6 requests/s within both latency targets. A prefill-only GPU sustained 5.6 req/s and a decode-only GPU 10 req/s. What per-GPU rate could 2 prefill GPUs plus 1 decode GPU reach?
blocks.reveal: Two prefill GPUs give 2 x 5.6 = 11.2 req/s of prefill capacity, so the single decode GPU (10 req/s) becomes the limit: **10 req/s over 3 GPUs, about 3.3 req/s per GPU**. That is roughly 2.1x the colocated 1.6 req/s, from the same hardware, just by not making the phases share a GPU. This back-of-envelope example in the DistServe introduction is the whole idea of disaggregation in one line.

blocks.md: There is a second, quieter problem: **coupled resources**. When both phases share GPUs they must share one parallelism plan and one GPU count, sized for whichever latency target is harder. Prefill wants more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT; decode's best plan depends on its batch size. DistServe argues that colocated systems end up over-provisioning to satisfy both.

Misconception: "interference only matters at high load." In the timeline there was just one new prompt. Any long prompt that lands in a decode iteration creates a stall for every request in the batch. Load makes it more frequent, not possible.
Prefill is compute-bound and sets TTFT; decode is memory-bound and sets TPOT. Putting both in one batch makes each phase pay for the other.

blocks.question: In the toy model, a decode step for 16 requests costs 18.2 ms. A 4096-token prompt would join the next iteration in full. Roughly how long would the 16 running requests wait for their next token?
options: About 18 ms, because decode is memory-bound and unaffected
About 411 ms, because the iteration now costs max(18.2, 0.1 x 4112)
About 36 ms, two decode steps
About 104 ms, the same as for a 1024-token prompt
blocks.explain: The iteration time is set by the slower of math and memory. 4096 prompt tokens plus 16 decode tokens is 4112 tokens of math, 0.1 x 4112 = 411.2 ms, which dominates 18.2 ms. The stall scales with prompt length, which is exactly what DistServe's Figure 2 shows.

blocks.question: Which metric does a chat user notice first if prefills are always scheduled ahead of decodes on a busy colocated GPU?
options: TTFT gets worse
Neither, since prefill priority helps everyone
TPOT/TBT gets worse: running streams stutter while new prompts are processed
Throughput in tokens per second must drop
blocks.explain: Prioritizing prefill keeps TTFT low but every prefill iteration delays the next token of every running request. Splitwise notes that letting a waiting prompt preempt token generation shortens TTFT but can substantially increase the tail of TBT. Throughput may even rise; latency of the other phase is what suffers.

lessons.title: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs

blocks.md:
Raw throughput (tokens or requests per second) rewards a server that keeps the GPU full, even if half the users stare at a frozen stream. DistServe instead optimizes **goodput**: the highest request rate a deployment can sustain while a target fraction of requests meet *both* latency targets.

The targets are **SLOs** (service level objectives), such as TTFT at most 400 ms and TPOT at most 25 ms. **SLO attainment** is the fraction of requests that meet all of them. DistServe's experiments use a 90% attainment goal (and report 99% in an appendix).

blocks.caption: lambda is the arrival rate in requests per second. Dividing by the GPU count makes a 3-GPU design comparable with a 1-GPU design, which is why it maps to cost per query.

blocks.md: Start with a tiny example. Eight requests were served (made-up measurements) with SLOs TTFT at most 400 ms and TPOT at most 25 ms. A request counts only if it meets both.

scenes.caption: The raw measurements. The SLOs are TTFT at most 400 ms and TPOT at most 25 ms.
Check TTFT: the requests at index 3 and 6 are too slow (450 and 520 ms). TTFT attainment alone is 6/8 = 75%.
Check TPOT: the request at index 4 streams too slowly (31 ms per token). TPOT attainment alone is 7/8 = 87.5%.
Joint attainment counts requests that pass both: 5/8 = 62.5%. That is below 90%, so this rate is above the goodput of the deployment, even though each metric alone looks decent.

blocks.md:
To find goodput you sweep the arrival rate, measure attainment at each rate, and take the largest rate still at or above 90%. DistServe does this with a simulator fitted to the model's prefill and decode latency (its paper reports under 2% error against real runs) and binary search, because testing every configuration on real GPUs is too slow.

The figure below comes from a toy discrete-event simulation run for this course: Poisson arrivals, every prompt 1024 tokens, 128 output tokens, SLOs of 400 ms TTFT and 25 ms TPOT, and the same made-up iteration cost as lesson 1. The rates are *per GPU*, so the 3-GPU disaggregated setup is offered three times the total traffic.

blocks.title: Toy simulation: SLO attainment vs per-GPU request rate

scenes.caption: One colocated GPU with full prefills mixed into decode batches. Attainment falls below 90% between 2 and 2.5 req/s, mostly from TPOT misses caused by prefill stalls. Its goodput is 2.4 req/s.
Two prefill GPUs plus one decode GPU (2P1D), offered three times the traffic. It stays above 90% up to about 4.3 req/s per GPU (13.0 req/s in total), so per-GPU goodput is 4.33.

blocks.md: Goodput is not throughput. A colocated GPU at 4 req/s still produces plenty of tokens per second, but in the toy run only 29% of requests meet both SLOs. If you only tracked throughput, that overloaded point would look like the best one.

Real SLOs depend on the application. DistServe set them per workload: a chatbot on OPT-13B used 0.25 s TTFT and 0.1 s TPOT; code completion on OPT-66B used a tight 0.125 s TTFT; summarization of long documents used a loose 15 s TTFT but a 0.15 s TPOT. Tight TTFT pushes resources toward prefill; tight TPOT pushes them toward decode. Mooncake (Moonshot AI's serving system for Kimi) frames the same goal as maximizing throughput under TTFT and TBT SLOs, and counts only requests that fully complete.
Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

blocks.question: System A serves 9 req/s on 3 GPUs at 92% attainment. System B serves 4 req/s on 1 GPU at 91% attainment, and 4.5 req/s at 85%. Assuming these are the largest rates meeting 90%, which has higher per-GPU goodput?
options: A, because 9 req/s is more than 4 req/s
B, with 4.5 req/s per GPU
They tie, since both exceed 90%
B, with 4 req/s per GPU against A's 3
blocks.explain: Per-GPU goodput divides the highest rate meeting the attainment goal by the GPU count: A gives 9/3 = 3 req/s per GPU and B gives 4/1 = 4. B's 4.5 req/s point misses the 90% goal, so it does not count.

blocks.question: Your summarization service has a 15 s TTFT SLO and a 0.15 s TPOT SLO. Attainment is failing. Which change most likely helps?
options: Give prefill more tensor parallelism to cut TTFT
Lower the TTFT SLO to 5 s
Protect decode steps from long prefills (separate decode GPUs or smaller prefill chunks)
Batch more prompts into each prefill
blocks.explain: With a 15 s TTFT budget, prefill is rarely the binding constraint. The long documents create long prefills that stall decode steps and break the TPOT SLO, which DistServe observed for vLLM on LongBench. Shielding decode is the fix; batching more prompts would make the stalls worse.

lessons.title: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism

blocks.md: Disaggregation gives each phase its own GPUs. DistServe calls a unit that holds one full copy of the weights an **instance** (one GPU or many with model parallelism). A **prefill instance** only runs prompts and produces the first token; a **decode instance** receives the request's KV cache and generates the rest. Splitwise (Patel et al., ISCA 2024) builds the same split from machine pools and calls the phases *prompt* and *token*.

blocks.title: A request through a disaggregated deployment

scenes.caption: Two prefill instances feed one decode instance, the 2:1 ratio from DistServe's introduction. The pools are sized separately.
DistServe's controller sends each new request to the prefill instance with the shortest queue. Prefill computes the prompt's KV cache and the first token.
The KV cache moves to the least-loaded decode instance. In DistServe the decode side pulls it when it has room, so the prefill GPU's memory acts as the queue during bursts.
The decode instance adds the request to its continuous batch and streams tokens. It never runs a prefill, so its steps stay short and steady.

blocks.md: Once the phases are apart, each can be tuned for its own SLO. DistServe analyzes a prefill instance as an **M/D/1 queue** (Poisson arrivals at rate $R$, a fixed service time $D$, one server), which gives the average TTFT in closed form. It then compares two ways to use 2 GPUs: **inter-op** (pipeline) parallelism, which keeps the time per request about $D$ but doubles capacity, and **intra-op** (tensor) parallelism, which cuts the time to $D/K$ for a speedup $1 < K < 2$ lost partly to communication.

blocks.caption: DistServe equations 1 to 3. First term: execution time. Second term: queueing delay, which explodes as the server nears full utilization.

blocks.title: Prefill TTFT on 2 GPUs: pipeline vs tensor parallelism

scenes.caption: D = 0.1 s, K = 1.6. At low rates tensor parallelism wins (0.067 s vs 0.103 s at R = 2) because execution time dominates. Past about 11 req/s pipeline wins because queueing dominates.
With a better speedup K = 1.9, tensor parallelism stays ahead over the plotted range. A tight TTFT SLO or fast interconnect favors intra-op; DistServe searches this space automatically.

blocks.md: DistServe turns this into a placement search. For each phase it enumerates parallelism configurations, uses its simulator to find the highest rate meeting the SLO attainment target, keeps the best per-GPU goodput, and then replicates instances to match the traffic. For OPT-175B on ShareGPT it chose prefill with inter-op 3 and intra-op 3, and decode with inter-op 3 and intra-op 4, a plan a human would rarely guess. The search took under 1.3 minutes in their largest setting.

blocks.title: Toy simulation: per-GPU goodput by pool ratio

scenes.caption: Same toy workload as lesson 2. Colocated: 2.4 req/s per GPU. A 1:1 split reaches 5.9 req/s on 2 GPUs, only 2.95 per GPU, because the prefill GPU limits TTFT while the decode GPU sits partly idle.

2P1D reaches 13.0 req/s on 3 GPUs (4.33 per GPU). 3P1D adds a GPU but the decode GPU becomes the limit: 13.5 req/s on 4 GPUs, 3.38 per GPU. 3P2D gives 22.2 on 5, 4.44 per GPU. The ratio matters as much as the split.

blocks.md: Splitwise adds a hardware angle. Its characterization on Azure production traces found that token generation barely uses the compute of the newest GPUs: with power capped by half (700 W to 350 W per H100), the token phase saw almost no latency impact while the prompt phase slowed a lot. So Splitwise-HA uses H100 machines for prompts and A100 machines for tokens, and Splitwise-HHcap power-caps the token machines. The paper reports up to 1.4x higher throughput at 20% lower cost, or 2.35x more throughput for the same cost and power budget.

Splitwise also keeps a **mixed pool**: machines borrowed from the prompt or token pool run both phases with mixed batching when load shifts, then return to their pool. This softens the fragmentation that a fixed prefill:decode ratio would otherwise cause.

blocks.question: A disaggregated deployment meets TTFT easily but misses TPOT at high load, and decode GPUs are near their KV memory limit. What is the most sensible next change?
options: Add prefill instances
Add decode capacity (more decode instances or more parallelism per decode instance)
Merge the pools back into a colocated deployment
Increase the prefill batch size
blocks.explain: TPOT is decided by the decode side. Decode batch size is bounded by KV memory, and DistServe notes that scaling the decoding instance with model parallelism (or memory techniques like PagedAttention and GQA) lets it batch more. Extra prefill instances would just send more KV caches to an already full decode pool.

blocks.question: Using DistServe's equations with D = 0.1 s and K = 1.6, which 2-GPU plan gives lower average TTFT at a low arrival rate of 2 req/s?
options: Intra-op (tensor): it cuts execution time to D/K, and queueing is small at low rate
Inter-op (pipeline): it doubles capacity
They are identical at low rate
Neither; one GPU is always better
blocks.explain: At R = 2 the intra-op TTFT is 0.0625 + 0.0045 = about 0.067 s, while inter-op is 0.1 + 0.0028 = about 0.103 s. Execution time dominates at low load, so cutting it wins. At high load the queueing term flips the order.

lessons.title: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap

blocks.md: Disaggregation's price is that the KV cache built by prefill must reach the decode GPU before the second token. Splitwise calls this transfer the main overhead of the design. How big is it? From the KV cache course, each token stores one key and one value vector per layer per KV head.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes/token} = 2 \times L \times H_{kv} \times d_{head} \times b,\qquad t_{transfer} = \frac{\text{prompt tokens} \times \text{bytes/token}}{\text{link bandwidth}}
blocks.caption: L layers, H_kv key/value heads, d_head head size, b bytes per element (2 for BF16 or FP16). Real transfers add setup and protocol overhead, so this is a lower bound.

blocks.md:
Worked example with Qwen3-32B, whose published config has 64 layers, 8 KV heads (grouped-query attention) and head size 128, stored in BF16:

- bytes per token: $2 \times 64 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 262{,}144$ B = 256 KiB
- an 8192-token prompt: $8192 \times 262{,}144 = 2{,}147{,}483{,}648$ B = 2 GiB (about 2.15 GB)

Over three links, ignoring overhead: 25 Gb/s Ethernet (3.125 GB/s) takes 687 ms; a 400 Gb/s InfiniBand NIC (50 GB/s) takes 43 ms; NVLink between A100s at the 600 GB/s peak DistServe quotes takes 3.6 ms.

blocks.title: Ideal KV transfer time vs prompt length

scenes.caption: At 400 Gb/s an 8192-token Qwen3-32B prompt moves in 43 ms. OPT-66B uses full multi-head attention (72 KV heads of 128 in 64 layers), so the same prompt carries 9x more bytes.
At 25 Gb/s, DistServe's cross-node bandwidth, even Qwen3-32B needs 687 ms for 8192 tokens. Sending KV across such a link at full size would eat most of a typical TTFT budget.
At 1600 Gb/s the Qwen3-32B transfer for 8192 tokens drops to about 11 ms. Bandwidth, the model's KV layout, and prompt length decide whether the transfer matters.

blocks.md:
Check the formula against DistServe: OPT-66B has 64 layers and hidden size 9216, so a token takes $2 \times 64 \times 9216 \times 2 = 2{,}359{,}296$ B and a 512-token request takes 1.125 GiB, the paper's "approximately 1.13GB". At 10 requests per second that is 11.25 GiB/s, or 90 Gib/s of sustained bandwidth, the paper's 90 Gbps.

That gives two separate checks for any link: **latency** (does one transfer fit inside the TTFT and TPOT budgets?) and **throughput** (can the link sustain request rate times KV bytes?). A 400 Gb/s link moves at most about 23 Qwen3-32B 8K-token caches per second; a 25 Gb/s link about 1.5.

The latency check gets much easier with **layer-wise streaming**. Each layer's KV cache is final as soon as that layer's prefill finishes, so it can be sent while the next layers compute. Splitwise does exactly this for large prompts (serial transfer for small ones), and Mooncake streams each layer's KV to the decode node while prefill continues. The figure groups the 64 layers into 4 blocks of 16 for readability.

blocks.title: Serialized vs layer-wise transfer (8K prompt, 25 Gb/s)

scenes.caption: Serialized: prefill (estimated 1454 ms, see below) finishes, then the whole 2 GiB crosses the 25 Gb/s link in 687 ms. Decode cannot start until 2141 ms.
Layer-wise in 4 groups: each group's KV (172 ms) is sent while the next group computes (364 ms). Only the last group's send is exposed: decode can start at 1626 ms.

Per layer, the exposed tail shrinks to one layer's KV: 33.5 MB, about 10.7 ms at 25 Gb/s. Splitwise measured a near-constant non-overlapped time of about 8 ms (A100) and 5 ms (H100) with this optimization.

blocks.md: The prefill time in the figure is an estimate, not a measurement: Qwen3-32B has about 31.2B non-embedding parameters, so an 8192-token prefill needs about $2 \times 31.2\text{B} \times 8192 \approx 511$ TFLOP of matrix math plus about 70 TFLOP of causal attention. At an assumed sustained 400 TFLOP/s that is about 1.45 s, or 22.7 ms per layer, longer than the 10.7 ms per-layer transfer, so the stream keeps up.

Overlap hides latency, not bandwidth. If two prefill GPUs share that 25 Gb/s link and each finishes an 8K prompt every 1.45 s, they produce about 1.4 caches/s against a link that sustains about 1.5. Add a third and the link becomes the bottleneck, however well transfers overlap.

Placement manages the bandwidth check. DistServe's testbed had NVLink inside each 8-GPU node but only 25 Gbps between nodes, so its low node-affinity algorithm splits each instance into pipeline stages and puts the prefill and decode segments of the *same* stage in one node; KV for a layer then only moves over NVLink. Even for OPT-175B, transfer was under 0.1% of total latency and over 95% of requests waited less than 30 ms.

**Mooncake** makes the KV cache the center of the design. It pools the GPU cluster's underused CPU, DRAM and SSD resources into a disaggregated KV cache, moves blocks with an RDMA-based component (Messenger; RDMA lets a network card read or write another machine's memory without that machine's CPU), and its global scheduler (Conductor) picks a prefill node partly by how much of the prompt's prefix is already cached there. It reports up to 525% more throughput in simulated long-context cases and 75% more requests for Kimi on real workloads.

Today the transport is usually a library. **NIXL** (NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library) provides point-to-point transfers across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage through plug-in backends such as UCX; NVIDIA Dynamo and vLLM's `NixlConnector` use it.

blocks.code:
# vLLM docs example (same host): one prefiller and one decoder
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5600 \
  vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --port 8100 --enforce-eager \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail"}'

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT=5601 \
  vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --port 8200 --enforce-eager \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_load_failure_policy":"fail"}'

# a proxy sends each request to the prefiller first, then the decoder
python tests/v1/kv_connector/nixl_integration/toy_proxy_server.py --port 8192 \
  --prefiller-hosts localhost --prefiller-ports 8100 \
  --decoder-hosts localhost --decoder-ports 8200
blocks.caption: From vLLM's NixlConnector usage guide. The decoder reads KV blocks from the prefiller; the prefiller holds them under a lease (default 30 s) until they are read.

blocks.md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

blocks.question: Using the formula, how long does an ideal transfer of a 4096-token Qwen3-32B prompt (256 KiB per token) take over a 400 Gb/s link?
options: About 2.7 ms
About 172 ms
About 344 ms
About 21.5 ms
blocks.explain: 4096 x 262,144 B = 1,073,741,824 B (1 GiB). 400 Gb/s is 50 GB/s, so 1.074 GB / 50 GB/s = 21.5 ms. Half of the 43 ms needed for 8192 tokens, because KV size grows linearly with prompt length.

blocks.question: A team streams KV layer by layer, so per-request exposed transfer is only 10 ms. At peak, prefill GPUs produce 40 GB/s of KV, and the shared link carries 25 GB/s. What happens?
options: Nothing, because overlap already hid the transfer
TTFT rises slightly but TPOT is unaffected
Transfers queue up without bound: the link cannot sustain the KV production rate, so decode starts slip further and prefill memory fills
Decode GPUs simply run larger batches
blocks.explain: Overlap hides one transfer behind compute, but sustained bandwidth must still exceed rate x KV bytes. At 40 GB/s produced against 25 GB/s carried, the backlog grows. DistServe's 90 Gbps example is exactly this throughput check.

lessons.title: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins

blocks.md:
Disaggregation is not the only fix for interference. **Sarathi-Serve** (Agrawal et al., OSDI 2024) keeps both phases on the same GPUs and changes how batches are built:

- **Chunked prefill**: split a long prompt into chunks processed over several iterations.
- **Stall-free batching**: each iteration first packs every running decode, then fills the remaining **token budget** with prefill chunks, so decodes never wait for a whole prompt.

The budget is chosen from the TBT SLO by profiling: the largest number of tokens per iteration that still meets it.

Why is this cheap? Decode iterations are memory-bound, so they leave arithmetic idle. A prefill chunk of a few hundred tokens fills that slack. Sarathi-Serve reports up to 2.6x higher serving capacity than vLLM for Mistral-7B on one A100 and up to 3.7x for Yi-34B on two A100s. The figure replays lesson 1's arrival with three designs, using the same made-up cost model.

blocks.title: Prompt C arrives at 30 ms: three designs

scenes.caption: Colocated, full prefill (lesson 1): the 16 running requests wait 104 ms for one token. C's TTFT is 110.4 ms.
Chunked, budget 256: each iteration holds 16 decodes plus a 240-token chunk and costs 25.6 ms. Decodes see 25.6 ms gaps instead of a 104 ms stall; C's TTFT grows to 127.0 ms.
Disaggregated: C's prefill runs alone on its own GPU (TTFT 102.4 ms), its KV moves in 5.4 ms (1024 tokens at 50 GB/s), and decode steps never change from 18.2 ms. C joins the batch at 145.6 ms.

blocks.md: Chunking has costs. DistServe argues it only mitigates interference: small chunks underuse the GPU and stretch TTFT, large chunks leave little room for decodes, and every chunk must re-read the KV cache of all earlier chunks. Sarathi-Serve agrees the extra reads exist but finds attention prefill stays compute-bound even at small chunk sizes, so the overhead is small in practice. The hard part is picking the budget: the vLLM docs say chunked prefill with a proper chunk size can control tail ITL too, "but in practice it's hard to figure out the correct chunk size value".

blocks.title: Toy simulation: per-GPU goodput, chunked vs disaggregated

scenes.caption: Same toy workload as lessons 2 and 3 (1024-token prompts, 128 output tokens, SLOs 400 ms and 25 ms). A budget of 128 is too small for TTFT; 512 is too large for TPOT.

Tuned well (192 to 256), one chunked GPU reaches 5.7 req/s, above the best disaggregated ratio's 4.44 per GPU. Simplified: the toy charges nothing for chunking, uses short prompts, and gives disaggregation no per-phase parallelism or hardware edge.

blocks.prompt: The toy shows chunked prefill beating disaggregation, yet DistServe reports up to 7.4x more requests (or 12.6x tighter SLOs) than vLLM and its chunked-prefill baseline DeepSpeed-MII. What does the toy leave out that the paper exploits?
blocks.reveal: The toy gives every design identical 1-GPU instances. DistServe's wins come largely from **choosing different parallelism and GPU counts per phase** (for example tensor parallelism for a tight TTFT), from **long prompts** where chunks multiply KV reloads and decode stalls, and from **tight SLOs on both metrics at once**. Splitwise adds **different hardware per phase**. The toy is honest about one thing: on a small model with short prompts, a well-tuned colocated scheduler is a strong baseline.

blocks.md:
How the sources draw the line:

- **Disaggregation tends to win** with long prompts, strict TTFT and TPOT SLOs together, large models that need different parallelism per phase, enough GPUs to size pools, and a fast KV fabric (NVLink or RDMA). DistServe also argues long context helps: prefill compute grows faster than KV size.
- **Colocation (with chunked prefill) tends to win** for throughput-oriented offline jobs, few GPUs, small models, short prompts, or slow interconnects. DistServe's own discussion says chunked prefill may be preferred in offline settings, and simpler non-disaggregated systems in resource-constrained ones.

The vLLM docs add one more note: disaggregated prefill "DOES NOT improve throughput". Its point is controlling TTFT and tail ITL separately.

Production systems blur the line. NVIDIA **Dynamo** runs vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM workers in separate prefill and decode pools, moves KV with NIXL, and its docs state disaggregation "is not automatically better": for small models, short prompts, low concurrency or no fast KV-transfer fabric, aggregated serving is simpler and often faster. Its experimental **conditional disaggregation** sends a request to remote prefill only when needed: if the prompt minus the prefix already cached on the chosen decode worker is short enough (default threshold 2048 tokens), the decode worker prefills it locally. Mooncake similarly chunks very long prefills and splits them across prefill nodes.

Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill.

Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

blocks.question: An offline batch job summarizes millions of documents overnight. There is no latency SLO; the goal is tokens per dollar. Which design do the sources point toward?
options: Disaggregation, because it always raises goodput
Colocated serving with chunked prefill to keep every iteration near the compute-bound point
Disaggregation over 25 Gb/s Ethernet to save NVLink
Separate prefill and decode clusters on different GPU generations, mandatory for throughput
blocks.explain: Goodput only matters when there are SLOs. DistServe's discussion says that in throughput-oriented offline settings, chunked prefill with piggybacking may be preferred because it fills each batch to the compute-bound threshold. vLLM's docs also note disaggregated prefill does not improve throughput.

blocks.question: Under Dynamo's conditional disaggregation (isl_bounding policy, default threshold 2048 tokens), a 6000-token chat turn arrives and 5000 of its tokens are already cached on the chosen decode worker. Assuming the ratio condition also passes, where is it prefilled?
options: On the decode worker itself, since only about 1000 uncached tokens remain
On a remote prefill worker, because 6000 exceeds 2048
It is rejected
It is split between both pools
blocks.explain: The policy looks at effective input length: the prompt minus the cached prefix overlap on the selected decode worker, here 1000 tokens, below the 2048 default. The decode worker prefills locally, saving a KV transfer and remote prefill work. The default ratio threshold is 0.7, and 1000/6000 is about 0.17, so the ratio check passes too.
